Let's talk about 2FA (two factor authentication), would it still allow automatic login if you have your passwords saved in the browser?

The typical implementation two factor authentication is that it requires a specific code that constantly rotates and can't be saved. You have to prove that you have control over an authorized device by supplying whatever matching code that device generates at a given interval.

You can usually set an authorized device to stop requiring the 2FA code after the first login, but exploiting that fact would require a hacker to have physical or remote access to your authorized device.

AMA about technology, politics relating to technology, tech support, the show, or whatever.

Hey, thanks! We love having tech savvy people on board with us. It definitely makes for some interesting conversations, especially when we get into the more nefarious topics like what the NSA / FBI / Alphabet Agencies are trying to slip into law regarding encryption and the like.
I'd love to be able to contribute to the conversation somehow!

There are lots of ways! You can listen to the show live via the web stream at http://www.gurushow.com, where there's a chat feature that we monitor during the show. You can also email us at radio@azcomputerguru.com with your thoughts or questions. You can call the station during the show as well, but it might be better to wait until we get our 800 number up for that (soon now that we're posting the show online).

The main thing is that we encourage people to give us their opinions, even (and especially) when they disagree. We love having interesting and thought provoking conversations with listeners.
That sounds awesome, thanks for sharing! My question: what was one unanticipated effect of branching out from radio into internet podcasting?

Awesome question! One thing we've noticed since taking that first step is that our audience is no longer only one or two demographics, but instead it's pretty much all of them. Although 80,000 listeners represents a lot of people, since those listeners are largely ones who listen to the station we're on anyway, they fit into one major demographic and then a few subdemographics from there. On the internet, however, we have the chance to put our show in front of everyone, all at once.

While this is scary, it's also awesome. There are things we have wanted to do with the show for a long time now, but most of those things aren't possible without expanding to the internet. We want to run extra shows which would be long-format so that we can get deeper into subjects than we could on the radio, but being on the radio is insanely expensive, so right now we can't expand the radio show. On the internet, however, we can make extra shows which are as long as we want and talk about whatever we want.

So it's invigorating! We're trying to see what the interest in our show is like so we can hopefully start producing even more content and talking about a lot more subjects at length. Thanks for the question!

It sounds like you're meeting the new-found variety of audience with variety of content, which sounds like an excellent approach to me. I hadn't considered how moving from radio to podcasts would "de-homogenize" your audience further, but it makes sense when I consider it. It's amazing to realize that in someways radio is becoming the niche medium and podcasting the more mainstream, although it sounds like you're doing a good job of staying ahead of that curve without detracting from your existing audience. I wish you the best of luck and thanks again for the AMA!
